Question: How did you handle failure?
Answer: As we all know, failure is never fun. But keep in mind that how I deal with it really depends on the specific situation. In some cases, I’d just move on. Most failure are not catastrophic, after all. When I was younger, and single, if I asked a girl out and she said “no” than I’d move on and ask someone else. I take the same position at work. If I proposed an idea, and its rejected, I just move on to something else. There are plenty of ideas that will follow. In other words, I don't hang all of my self-esteem on just one event. Now, if the failure is a project, as in the prototype did work, then it became a chance to learn. To do a deep dive and analyze why it failed. And again, a failure or setback of this nature does not derail the entire project. Infact, you want to be agile: fail fast! Then learn all you can't and try again, applying all of the lessons learned. To quote Hannibal Smith: The Opera is not over until the fat lady sings! To expand on this idea here, is don't quit too early. Some people are good at snatching defeat out of the jaws of victory. I’m not one of them. Now, in some cases there is the “sunk cost” fallacy in which you keep pouring time & money into a doomed project. There are times to give up. If that's the case, I just move on. But again, sometimes you learn the most from such failures, so keep that in mind. You can't unlearn something. The IBM “stretch” computer in the early 60’s was a commercial failure, but 80% of its design was used in the System 360 (which is considered one of the most successful products of all time). So, i believe that a single failure is not the end of the world! It can set you up for something better, if you have the right mindset.

Question: What contributed to the rise of the personal computer?
Answer: Several things were needed for the “rise” of personal computers. The invention of the microprocessor was vital, and probably goes without saying. The advent of relatively low-cost microprocessors made “home computers” possible. Closely related were low-cost memory chips. And while I like more conventional static RAM, it was dynamic RAM that made memory cheap. Nevertheless, early computers had very limited amounts of memory. In the early 80, it was not uncommon for a computer to have 16k of RAM, with upgrades available for (way) more money. That was one reason why the commodore 64 was such a big hit. The biggest problem between early computers was lack of compatibility. Each manufacturer had their own OS, and even worse, often different formats for floppy disks. So, you could not, for example, work on a document at home on your C64 and take it to work and read the disk on an IBM PC. Because of this, I bought my first MS-DOS machine in 1989 ($1200 for a single floppy “Laser Compact XT” with 512k of ram. I later upgraded it to 640k and figured out how to make a floppy extension cable so I would have a B drive! Keep in mind that MS-DOS and the IBM architecture created a “safe, conservative” environment for business users. The development of VisiCalc and work processers (WordStar) make the PC important to the office at work. There was even a early PC-version of AutoCAD (one of my professors even said he got a math coprocessor, which was also a thing). People don't think about this much, but the lowly dot matrix printer also was an important factor in the adoption of PC’s. It enabled the PC to replace the typewriter in the office, but also make computers useful for students (using word processors to write papers). I was one of them who went through that transition from typing papers to writing them using a word process (I used “Easy Writer” because it was cheap! It really was a game changer! The irony is many printers used the standard Centronics interface, or the RS-232 serial port. It was displaced in the late 90’s and early 2000s by USB, but unlike the floppy issue, there were fewer compatibility issues. I already alluded to software like WordStar and VisiCalc, but one can't overlook the fact that having commercial software that made a computer actually useful for most users was also vital to adopting a personal computer. Most people objection back them was “what am I going to use a computer for” and such software . The irony is very few people used then for storing recipes or creating “databases” for their stamp collection. Games were also a contributor, but dedicated game machine did the job better for many years. And while modems allowed users to connect to BBS systems, the world wide web is probably the tipping point for universal adoption. Web applications like shopping gave most people a reason to have a computer, hence the faster adoption rates in the late 90’s. It also gave rise to instant messaging & social media. Hence, you reading this answer. Been there, done that!

Question: What are the differences between the army and air force in terms of quality of life, benefits, salary and career opportunities?
Answer: First, your pay and benefits are controlled by congress, not the branches. An E-5 is an E-5 no matter what branch you serve in. Here is the enlisted pay scale from Military(.com). Note there is no branch of service indicated. And the same is true with BAQ/BAS and other allowances. So formal pay & benefits are the same. The Army used to have faster promotions, especially to E4 & E5. Some of that may be due to the Army in the 80’s had a two-year option. Maybe someone could elaborate, but in 1983–84 it took me 29 weeks as an E3 to make E4 (I know the USMC had a “terminal Lance” thing going on, but they were not part of the question). I was so upset that when I was able to test for E5, I studied like it was a college final. I even took CLEP & DANTES exams as “practice tests” to get me better prepared. It paid off, as I made E5 & E6 on my first attempt. As for career opportunities, there are two ways to view this: while active duty and after you leave the service. I’d assume that within certain career fields, you are going to have similar jobs. The Airforce had helicopters; the army has lots more. Yet the skills & training to maintain them would be similar. That includes avionics, engines (propulsion) and airframe. The largest difference is the Army has a whole bunch of combat careers, whereas the USAF does have a small number of security forces. The army would also have a much larger number of heavy equipment operators. So, while the USAF does have a higher percentage of technical jobs, that’s only a fraction of jobs that are available. The USAF does have a benefit of have its own community college, with each career fields having its own AAS degree. In fact, my first degree was through CCAF, in Avionics Systems Technology. Note this: Finding a job after leaving the military is almost never an easy task. Unless you're transferring into a civilian field that directly relates to your military experience, you will need to change fields in order to enter the civilian workforce (Bryan Wolfe) From BLS: The unemployment rate for veterans who served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces at any time since September 2001—a group referred to as Gulf War-era II veterans—was little changed at 3.3 percent in 2023 and the rate for all veterans was unchanged at 2.8 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. I picked my career based on the length of training, and the fact I was already interested in electronics and also wanted to work on aircraft. I knew these skills transferred, but also knew I wanted to earn a BS degree. You milage might vary, but for now we also have the GI Bill. I served in the 80’s so I was “between” GI bills, so it was essentially tuition assistance or bust. So, I left the USAF with a BS degree. With two kids by then I was not going to be able to go back to school that easily. Finally, about the quality of life. Again, there are several aspects to consider. The USAF is a military branch, it is still military, with lots of borrowed army traditions. The biggest issue with the Army (to me) would be the size of most bases. A typical 80-era fighter wing would have about 5000 airmen. So, you had hundreds of single airmen hitting the bars of the typical “small town” an Air Base would be located in. Many B-52 bases were northern tier (Maine, UP Michigan, the Dakotas) so that had an impact on a young person's social life. My first assignment was in Goldsboro NC, which seemed to be a bit too “small townish” for my liking, even though Raleigh was just an hour's drive away. My second was Clark Air Base was significantly different, to put it mildly. To put that in perspective, Pope AFB was co-located on what was then Fort Bragg, in Fayetteville NC. We nicknamed the town “fayette-nam.” And when I visited Fayetteville to see Ozzy Osborne, the town lived up to its name (nothing bad occurred, just observing everything around me). Take from this what you wish, as we all have different expectations in life. For example, even though the USAF was “better” in many regards, I still found as a 20-year-old plenty to complain about! Imagine that!

Question: I have an e-bike that’s 48V, 2,000 watts. Can I put a swap the current battery and controller for a 72V battery and a controller for more top speed?
Answer: While most electrical devices have a safety margin, its typically around 20-30%. This means that a device designed to operate at a certain voltage or current will be rated for 20-30% higher than its maximum expected operating conditions. The reason why in this case is that the motor is designed for a certain amount of mechanical force at a particular voltage, as well as an RPM. It is also designed for heat dissipation based on its maximum power input, so if we apply nearly twice the voltage, even if it creates no other damage, it will quickly overheat. Now, 72 volts in a 48-volt system is not quite doubling the voltage, it could also exceed the voltage rating of any internal components, especially electrolytic capacitors (provided it was a brushless motor, and had some integrated electronics) Note a 2000 watt electric motor on a eBike is already quite powerful. Question: How would you explain the Dilbert Principle to someone who’s never heard of it before?
Answer: First, we need to make sure they know of the earlier Peter Principle, as they are related but have one major difference. As for the Peter Principle, it's based on the premise that most organizations will reward their best workers with promotions into a supervisory role. But there the kicker, while some companies have working supervisors (at the lowest management level) many do not. In other words, you took you best mechanic and made them your shop manager. Now, they will better understand the day-to-day issues mechanics experience, or even help someone solve a problem. But they could really suck at the management part of the job. So, according to the Peter Principle, most to rise up to the level where they become incompetent and remain there. The Dilbert principle takes this a step farther: companies tend to promote incompetent employees to management to minimize their ability to harm productivity. So, the Peter Principle promotes people to their level to incompetence, where they stop. In the Dilbert Principle, it actually intentional. Put them in a role that does the least harm. Question: My girlfriend cheated on me after a 4 year relationship. I can't reconcile with the fact that she slept with someone else, considering we had only been with each other before this. Will I be able to forget with time? Do we have a future?
Answer: Whether you have a future depends on her attitude towards that mistake. You have made it clear that you were deeply hurt though. And quite frankly it's your decision to move on or work on the relationship. Don't let anyone try to push you into a decision. It's your pain, deal with it your own way. The pain will lessen with time, but the rate of change is also deeply personal. I didn't date for nearly two years after my 10-year marriage broke up. I didn't even meet my current wife until my ex wife got married. One tip: do find a friend who been there and will listen. If they have some advice or suggestions do consider them, but again make sure it's your decision. When I went through my divorce one of my friends was also going through one as well. We hung out almost every Sunday afternoon and had a pizza while watching a game on TV. It helped a lot (and I don't even like sports!)

Question: Which is better, MS Industrial and Systems Engineering or MS Engineering Management?
Answer: To me it depends on where you are at in your career. Plus, I am going out on a limb here and assume you already have a BS in ISE (or at least in an engineering discipline). If that is the case, I’d recommend to all college students working on their four-year degree to get a masters degree in their field vs management. One reason is that a 22-year-old is not ready for a management role, so it will be years until you would even be considered for management. I also recommend that the first 10 years or so is spent on the technical side of your career. You earned an engineering degree, be an engineer! You were not a business major, after all! Now, after you are in your mid-to-late 30’s, it's time to consider your future roles. By then you should be in some sort of senior engineering role, you might have even have lead projects. In my case, I did not get a MBA or engineering management degree, but I went ahead and earned my PMP. Just remember that moving up also makes you a prime candidate for the Peter Principle. However, we are also speaking of earning degrees, so you are not just some mechanic suddenly promoted without any preparation. But still, the job of management is fundamentally different.

Question: Why does my laundry room smell like a sewer? What can be done to get the smell out?
Answer: Your laundry room smells like a sewer because you are literally smelling the sewer. The purpose of a p- or s-trap is to prevent orders from passing through the plumbing. It does so by using water to block any gasses from the sewer from passing through. Here is a generic p-trap image from the internet: If someone connected the washer to a drain without a proper tap, you would have odors. You can also have issues if the traps dry out.
